GitHub Activity Analyzer

This report visualizes the liveliness of one or more GitHub projects over time. Every comment, pull request, review, and discussion contribution is tracked per contributor and per month, letting you spot activity trends, identify key contributors, and compare repositories side by side.

📊
Timeline

Aggregated monthly activity — the project's heartbeat at a glance. Switch between bar, line, and area views. Enable Split by Type to see Comments / PRs / Reviews stacked separately.

🏛️
Repo Comparison

When analyzing multiple repositories, this chart shows relative activity per repo over time. Use Stacked to see the total, Grouped to compare heights, or Line for trend comparison.

👥
Contributor Breakdown

Stacked bar chart showing how the top N contributors distribute their activity each month. Click any bar segment to open that contributor's personal drilldown.

🌡️
Heatmap

Calendar-style month grid colored by intensity. Filter to a single contributor to see their personal rhythm. Click any cell to filter the Leaderboard to that month.

🏆
Leaderboard

Ranked list of contributors by event count. Filter to any single month or use All Time. Repo chips show per-repository breakdown. Click a row to open the contributor drilldown.

🔍
Contributor Drilldown

Opens when you click a contributor anywhere. Shows their individual activity timeline, broken down by repository when multiple repos are loaded.

Tip: All filters (repo tab, event-type toggles) affect every chart simultaneously. The raw event data is embedded in this HTML file — no server needed, everything runs locally in your browser.

Filters & Toggles

Repo Tabs

The first toolbar row selects which repository's data is shown. ALL REPOS aggregates all loaded repositories; clicking a specific repo name narrows every chart to that repo only. The repo comparison chart is hidden when a single repo is selected.

Event-Type Toggles

The second toolbar row lets you include or exclude individual event types. Toggles are grouped into three categories:

CategoryToggleWhat it means
Comments issue commentA comment posted on any Issue or Pull Request thread
pr review commentAn inline code comment within a Pull Request diff
discussionA new Discussion thread opened in the repository
discussion commentA top-level reply inside a Discussion
discussion replyA nested reply to a discussion comment
commit commentA comment attached directly to a specific commit
Pull Requests pr openedA new Pull Request was opened by this contributor
pr mergedA Pull Request was merged — credited to the person who pressed Merge
pr closedA Pull Request was closed without merging
Reviews review approvedA review submitted with "Approve" verdict
review changes requestedA review submitted with "Request Changes" verdict
review commentedA review submitted with neutral "Comment" verdict (no verdict)

Shortcut Buttons

  • ALL ON / ALL OFF — enable or disable every event type at once.
  • Comments ONLY / Pull Requests ONLY / Reviews ONLY — instantly isolate one category and switch off all others. Useful for answering questions like "who writes the most code reviews?" without comment noise.
Note: Toggling event types is instantaneous — the full dataset is stored in the browser. No network requests are made after the page loads.

Event Types & Data Sources

The analyzer collects data from five GitHub API endpoints. Each event is attributed to the GitHub user who performed the action, tagged with the month it occurred, and stored with its event type.

What counts as an interaction?

The goal is to measure visible community contribution — actions that help other users, advance pull requests, or keep discussions moving. The following are deliberately not counted:

  • Commits (tracked separately in the contributor graph)
  • Reactions / emoji responses (no content contribution)
  • Bot accounts and the deleted "ghost" user

Attribution rules

EventCredited to
pr_openedThe author of the Pull Request
pr_mergedThe person who clicked Merge (merged_by), falling back to the PR author
pr_closedThe PR author (GitHub does not expose the closer via this endpoint)
review_*The reviewer who submitted the review
issue_commentThe comment author
pr_review_commentThe author of the inline diff comment
discussion / comment / replyThe respective author at each level
commit_commentThe comment author

Caching

After the first fetch, raw events are saved to .gh_cache_<owner>_<repo>.json next to the script. Subsequent runs load from cache instantly. Use --no-cache to force a full re-fetch (e.g. after new activity or after adding new event types).

Important: If you upgraded from an older version of this script that did not track PR and review events, you must run with --no-cache once to rebuild the cache with the full event set.

Command-Line Reference

The script requires Python 3.8+ and the requests library (pip install requests). A GitHub Personal Access Token (PAT) with at least public_repo scope is required.

Basic usage

python gh_activity.py <owner/repo> [owner/repo …] [options]

Arguments

ArgumentDescription
reposOne or more owner/repo strings. Multiple repos produce a combined report with cross-repo comparison.
--token TOKENGitHub Personal Access Token. Can also be set via the GH_TOKEN environment variable.
--since YYYY-MMOnly include data from this month onwards. Applied both during fetch and to cached data.
--out FILEOutput HTML filename. Defaults to owner_repo_activity.html (or a combined name for multiple repos).
--no-cacheIgnore existing cache files and re-fetch all data from the GitHub API.

Examples

# Single repository
python gh_activity.py open-quantum-safe/liboqs \
    --token $GH_TOKEN

# Multiple repos → one combined report
python gh_activity.py open-quantum-safe/liboqs \
                      open-quantum-safe/oqs-provider \
    --token $GH_TOKEN --since 2022-01

# Force refresh + custom output name
python gh_activity.py facebook/react facebook/relay \
    --token $GH_TOKEN --no-cache --out react_ecosystem.html

# Quick overview, last 12 months only
python gh_activity.py torvalds/linux \
    --token $GH_TOKEN --since 2024-01

Rate limits

The GitHub REST API allows 5,000 requests/hour for authenticated users. Large repositories with many PRs (thousands) may take 30–60 minutes on a first fetch. The script automatically pauses and retries when a rate limit is hit. Cache is saved incrementally per repo, so a partial run is safe to interrupt and resume (the interrupted repo will be re-fetched on the next run).

Token permissions

ScopeRequired for
public_repoAll public repository data
repoPrivate repositories (full scope needed)
GraphQLDiscussions — same token, no extra scope needed for public repos
